claim: Drosophila Hsl encodes a multifunctional lipid ester hydrolase with activity toward monoacylglycerol (MG), diacylglycerol (DG), triacylglycerol (TG), and steryl ester (SE).
source: Expression of His6-MmHsl increased cellular hydrolysis rates toward monoacylglycerol (MG), DG, TG, and SE by 6-, 9-, 6-, and 66-fold, respectively, as compared to His6-β-Gal expressing control cell extracts (Figure 1B). Expression of fly His6-Hsl elevated cellular hydrolysis rates toward MG, DG, TG, and SE by 14-, 16-, 10-, and 17-fold, respectively, as compared to His6-β-Gal expressing controls indicating a similar substrate spectrum of murine and fly Hsl (Figure 1B).
evidence: Recombinant Hsl expression in COS-7 cells increased hydrolase activities toward multiple lipid substrates as measured by enzymatic assays and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hsl in vivo increases DG, TG, and SE hydrolase activities but not MG hydrolase activity.
source: Ectopic expression of Hsl increased DG, TG, and SE hydrolase activities of abdominal extracts by 7-, 2-, and 8-fold, respectively, when compared to control samples. In contrast, abdominal MG hydrolase activities were not significantly altered by Hsl expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: Transgenic flies expressing Hsl under Act5c-GAL4 control showed increased hydrolase activities in abdominal extracts as measured by enzymatic assays and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Hsl localizes to lipid droplets in Drosophila fat body cells.
source: Finally, we assessed the subcellular localization of a fluorescently-tagged version of Hsl (Hsl-EGFP) in fat body cells of adult flies and found that Hsl-EGFP concentrated at the surface of LDs (Figure 1D).
evidence: Confocal microscopy of Hsl-EGFP expressing fat body cells showed colocalization with lipid droplets as visualized in Figure 1D.

claim: Hsl1 mutant animals are viable and exhibit normal lipid droplet morphology in fat body tissue.
source: Homozygous Hsl1 mutant animals are viable and were used to address the function of the enzyme in TG metabolism. Inspection of mature adult Hsl1 mutant fat body tissue revealed no apparent difference in the size or abundance of LDs when compared to age-matched controls (Figure 2B).
evidence: Microscopy analysis of fat body tissue from Hsl1 mutants showed no morphological differences compared to controls as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Hsl1 mutant animals have normal whole-body TG and DG levels.
source: Consistently, whole-body TG and DG levels of these Hsl1 mutants were indistinguishable from age-matched controls (Figure 2C).
evidence: Shotgun mass spectrometry measurements showed no significant differences in TG and DG levels between Hsl1 mutants and controls as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Hsl1 mutants exhibit normal TG molecular species composition.
source: Species with 40–50 acyl carbon atoms and 0–3 double bonds accounted for >80% of the TG pool with comparable species distributions in both genotypes (Figure 2D).
evidence: UPLC-MS analysis revealed similar TG species distributions between Hsl1 mutants and controls as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Hsl1 mutants show normal expression of genes involved in TG storage regulation including bmm, Akh, plin1, and plin2.
source: The mRNA concentrations of bmm, Akh, perilipin1 (plin1), and perilipin2 (plin2) were similar in Hsl1 mutant and control animals arguing against a compensatory transcriptional dysregulation of these genes in response to Hsl deficiency (Figure 2E).
evidence: qPCR measurements showed no significant differences in mRNA levels of lipolytic genes between Hsl1 mutants and controls as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Hsl1 mutants are capable of starvation-induced TG mobilization.
source: In contrast, Hsl1 bmm1 or Hsl1 AkhA double mutants were capable of starvation-induced TG mobilization and largely resembled bmm1 or AkhA single mutants in their TG storage phenotypes (Figure 2F).
evidence: TG measurements in starved flies showed that Hsl1 mutants can mobilize TG during starvation as shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Hsl1 mutants have 26% higher glycogen levels compared to controls under ad libitum fed conditions.
source: Next, we more broadly assessed energy metabolism in Hsl1 mutant animals and found levels of free glycerol, free FAs, and glucose unchanged in ad libitum fed Hsl1 mutants as compared to age-matched control animals whereas glycogen levels were 26% higher in Hsl1 mutants as compared to controls (Figure 2G).
evidence: Colorimetric assays showed elevated glycogen levels in Hsl1 mutants compared to controls as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Hsl1 mutants exhibit similar heat dissipation rates as controls under both fed and starved conditions.
source: Microcalorimetry revealed similar heat dissipation rates of Hsl1 and control animals under ad libitum fed conditions. Upon fasting, control and Hsl1 mutant animals reduced heat dissipation rates by 40% and 46%, respectively, indicating similar whole-body bioenergetics in both genotypes (Figure 2H).
evidence: Microcalorimetry measurements showed comparable metabolic rates between Hsl1 mutants and controls as shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Hsl1 mutants have normal starvation resistance.
source: Also, the response of Hsl1 mutants to starvation stress, a sensitive readout of perturbed energy metabolism, was indistinguishable from controls (Figure 2I).
evidence: Survival analysis during starvation showed no significant difference between Hsl1 mutants and controls as shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Hsl1 mutants accumulate SE in an age-dependent manner, with 2.1-fold and 2.5-fold higher levels at 7 and 14 days after eclosion, respectively.
source: Compared to controls, SE levels of Hsl1 mutants were similar at 1 day after eclosion, but 2.1- and 2.5-fold higher at 7 days and 14 days, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: TLC analysis showed progressive SE accumulation in Hsl1 mutants over time as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Hslb24 mutant animals also exhibit SE overstorage.
source: SE overstorage was also observed in 7-days-old females and males homozygous for the genetically independent Hslb24 allele (Figure 3B; Bi et al., 2012).
evidence: TLC analysis of a second independent Hsl mutant allele confirmed SE accumulation as shown in Figure 3B, with citation to previous work by Bi et al., 2012.

claim: Hsl1 mutants have 24% lower neutral SE hydrolase activity in abdominal extracts.
source: Moreover, neutral SE hydrolase activity in Hsl1 abdominal extracts was 24% lower compared to controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: Enzymatic assays showed reduced SE hydrolase activity in Hsl1 mutant extracts as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Hsl1 mutants exhibit slower turnover of SE prelabeled with 14C-FAs or 3H-cholesterol.
source: Consistent with reduced SE hydrolysis Hsl1 mutants exhibited slower turnover rates of SE prelabeled with 14C-FAs or 3H-cholesterol (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Radiolabeling experiments showed reduced SE turnover in Hsl1 mutants as shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Turnover of free 3H-cholesterol is unaffected in Hsl1 mutants.
source: In contrast, turnover of free 3H-cholesterol was unaffected by impaired SE catabolism in Hsl1 mutant animals (Figure 3F).
evidence: Radiolabeling experiments showed normal free cholesterol turnover in Hsl1 mutants as shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Hsl1 mutants have normal total free sterol levels under ad libitum fed conditions.
source: In line with this observation, 7-days-old Hsl1 mutant animals exhibited unaltered levels of total free sterols when compared to age-matched controls suggesting that defective SE catabolism does not limit free sterols due to dietary sterol supply under ad libitum fed conditions (Figure 3G).
evidence: Shotgun mass spectrometry showed no difference in total free sterol levels between Hsl1 mutants and controls as shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Hsl1 mutants and controls have similar sterol composition dominated by ergosterol and β-sitosterol.
source: However, both Hsl1 and control animals showed a similar sterol composition dominated by ergosterol and β-sitosterol with lower levels of campesterol and stigmasterol and traces of brassicasterol, desmo-/zymosterol, and lanosterol (Figure 3G).
evidence: Shotgun mass spectrometry analysis showed similar sterol species distributions between Hsl1 mutants and controls as shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Hsl1 mutants show 1.8-fold increased magro mRNA levels.
source: We observed a 1.8-fold increase in magro mRNA levels in Hsl1 mutants as compared to controls, whereas expression of all other sterol metabolic genes investigated remained largely unaltered in response to Hsl-deficiency (Figure 3H).
evidence: qPCR measurements showed elevated magro expression in Hsl1 mutants as shown in Figure 3H.

claim: SE levels are increased in multiple body segments of Hsl1 mutants, with the highest accumulation in carcasses.
source: In comparison to controls, SE levels were increased 2.6-, 2.8-, 2.4-, and 6.8-fold in Hsl1 mutant heads, thoraces, abdomen, and carcasses, respectively. Hsl1 mutant animals accumulated SE at lower levels also in the intestine but not in ovaries (Figure 4A).
evidence: TLC analysis of dissected body parts showed tissue-specific SE accumulation in Hsl1 mutants as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Hsl deficiency does not cause lipid droplet accumulation in larval ring glands.
source: Moreover, Hsl deficiency did not provoke accumulation of LDs in the larval ring gland, a steroidogenic tissue with highly active sterol metabolism (Figure 4B).
evidence: Microscopy analysis showed no LD accumulation in ring glands of Hsl1 mutants as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ubiquitous or fat body-specific re-expression of Hsl rescues the SE overstorage phenotype of Hsl1 mutants.
source: Ubiquitous or fat body-specific re-expression of Hsl by means of the Act5c-GAL4 or FB-GAL4 driver, respectively, rescued the SE overstorage phenotype of Hsl1 mutant animals (Figure 4C).
evidence: TLC analysis of transgenic rescue experiments showed normalization of SE levels with fat body-specific Hsl expression as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Neuronal, intestinal, or oenocyte-specific re-expression of Hsl does not rescue the SE overstorage phenotype of Hsl1 mutants.
source: In contrast, neuronal, intestinal or oenocyte-specific re-expression of Hsl by means of elav-GAL4, Myo31DF-GAL4 or Desat1-GAL4 drivers, respectively, did not revert the SE overstorage phenotype of Hsl1 mutants suggesting that Hsl acts autonomously in the fat body to control the organismal SE levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: TLC analysis of tissue-specific rescue experiments showed that only fat body expression rescues SE accumulation as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hsl in the fat body of control flies decreases total body SE storage by 46%.
source: In line with this observation, ectopic expression of Hsl in the fat body of control flies decreased total body SE storage by 46% as compared to controls (Figure 4D).
evidence: TLC analysis showed reduced SE levels upon fat body-specific Hsl overexpression as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mice with adipocyte-specific HSL deficiency (AHKO) lack detectable HSL immunoreactivity in white adipose tissue depots but not in liver, kidney, or muscle.
source: As shown in Figure 4E, AHKO mice lack detectable HSL immunoreactivity in subcutaneous (SCAT), perigonadal (PGAT), and perirenal (PRAT) white adipose tissue depots but not in liver, kidney, or muscle.
evidence: Immunoblotting analysis showed tissue-specific loss of HSL protein in AHKO mice as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: AHKO mice have normal TG levels but accumulate 10-, 12-, and 14-fold more SE in SCAT, PGAT, and PRAT, respectively.
source: AHKO animals had similar amounts of TG as controls in their SCAT, PGAT, and PRAT but accumulated 10-, 12-, and 14-fold more SE, respectively, in these adipose tissue depots (Figure 4F).
evidence: Lipid measurements showed selective SE accumulation without TG changes in AHKO adipose tissue as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: SE accumulation in AHKO adipose tissue is associated with a 63% decrease in neutral SE hydrolase activity.
source: SE accumulation in AHKO adipose tissue depots was associated with a 63% decrease in neutral SE hydrolase activity as compared to controls (Figure 4G).
evidence: Enzymatic assays showed reduced SE hydrolase activity in AHKO adipose tissue as shown in Figure 4G.

claim: AHKO mice show 83% decreased Hmgcs1 mRNA and 4.8-fold increased Soat1 mRNA in perigonadal adipose tissue.
source: Notably, mRNA concentrations of the de novo cholesterol synthesis gene Hmgcs1 were decreased by 83% in PGAT of AHKO mice as compared to controls arguing for a dysregulation of adipocyte sterol metabolic gene expression upon disrupted SE hydrolysis. Conversely, mRNA concentrations of the sterol-O-acyltransferase gene Soat1 were increased by 4.8-fold, whereas Hmgcr, Srebp2, Star, Abca1 were similarly expressed in both genotypes (Figure 4H).
evidence: qPCR measurements showed altered expression of sterol metabolism genes in AHKO adipose tissue as shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Embryonic SE levels drop by 66% within 6-8 hours after egg laying in control embryos.
source: In controls, embryonic SE levels dropped by 66% within 6–8 hr after egg laying (AEL) and were almost undetectable at the end of embryogenesis (18–20 hr; Figure 5A).
evidence: TLC analysis showed rapid SE catabolism during embryogenesis in control animals as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Embryos completely devoid of Hsl exhibit strongly delayed SE catabolism with 1.6-, 4.0-, and 7.4-fold higher SE levels than controls at 0-2 hr, 6-8 hr, and 18-20 hr AEL, respectively.
source: Embryos completely devoid of Hsl exhibited strongly delayed SE catabolism resulting in 1.6-, 4.0-, and 7.4-fold higher SE levels than controls at 0–2 hr, 6–8 hr, and 18–20 hr AEL, respectively.
evidence: TLC analysis showed impaired SE catabolism in Hsl1 mutant embryos as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Maternal Hsl genotype determines embryonic SE catabolism.
source: Heterozygous embryos from Hsl1 mutant mothers and control fathers had 1.5-, 4.1-, and 4.1-fold higher SE levels than control embryos at 0–2 hr, 6–8 hr, and 18–20 hr AEL, respectively. In contrast, heterozygous embryos from Hsl1 mutant fathers and control mothers exhibited similar SE catabolism rates than control embryos (Figure 5A) suggesting that maternal rather than zygotic Hsl determines embryonic SE breakdown.
evidence: Reciprocal crosses showed that maternal genotype determines embryonic SE levels as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Hsl1 mutant embryos have lower free sterol content than controls throughout embryogenesis.
source: SE catabolism in control embryos correlated with an increase in free sterol content from 12.4 to 20.7 pmol per animal between 0–2 hr and 18–20 hr AEL. Hsl1 mutant embryos had lower free sterol content than controls throughout embryogenesis and exhibited a blunted increase from 7.8 to 11.6 pmol per animal between 0–2 hr and 18–20 hr AEL (Figure 5B).
evidence: Shotgun mass spectrometry showed reduced free sterol accumulation in Hsl1 mutant embryos as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Germline-specific re-expression of Hsl largely restores embryonic SE hydrolysis rates in Hsl1 mutants.
source: Enzyme assays revealed a 72% decrease in embryonic SE hydrolysis rates of Hsl1 as compared to control animals, which was largely reverted by re-expressing Hsl in the germline of mutant mothers (Figure 5C).
evidence: Enzymatic assays showed rescue of SE hydrolase activity with germline-specific Hsl expression as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Germline-specific expression of Hsl fully prevents SE accumulation in Hsl1 mutant embryos but not in mothers.
source: Germline-specific expression of Hsl fully prevented the SE accumulation in Hsl1 mutant embryos but not in mothers consistent with a germline-autonomous role of the enzyme in SE catabolism (Figure 5C).
evidence: TLC analysis showed tissue-autonomous rescue of embryonic but not maternal SE levels as shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Hsl1 mutant embryos have similar hatching rates as control embryos.
source: To investigate if defective sterol homeostasis affects success rate or speed of the embryonic development of Hsl1 mutants, we first measured hatching rates and found that under our experimental conditions a similar fraction of control and Hsl1 mutant embryos hatched into 1st instar larvae (Figure 5D).
evidence: Hatching rate measurements showed no difference between Hsl1 mutants and controls as shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Control and Hsl1 mutant embryos have similar metabolic rates during embryogenesis.
source: Between 4 hr and 24 hr AEL, thermal dissipation rates of control and Hsl1 mutant embryos increased from 138 nW to 188 nW and from 132 nW to 182 nW, respectively, indicating similar metabolic rates in both genotypes (Figure 5E).
evidence: Microcalorimetry measurements showed comparable heat dissipation in control and Hsl1 mutant embryos as shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Control and Hsl1 mutant embryos reach comparable developmental stages at 4-6 hr, 7-9 hr, and 12-14 hr AEL.
source: Moreover, immunostainings of the segment-polarity protein Engrailed revealed that control and Hsl1 mutant embryos reached comparable stages of embryogenesis at 4–6 hr, 7–9 hr, or 12–14 hr AEL (Figure 5F).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showed similar developmental progression in control and Hsl1 mutant embryos as shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Embryogenesis in control animals is associated with a gradual decrease in TG by 12% and 58% at 6-8 hr and 18-20 hr AEL, respectively.
source: In control animals, embryogenesis was associated with a gradual decrease in TG (by 12% and 58% at 6–8 hr and 18–20 hr AEL, respectively, compared to 0–2 hr AEL) but not DG (Figure 6A).
evidence: Shotgun mass spectrometry showed progressive TG depletion during embryogenesis as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Major glycerophospholipids including PC, PE, PI, and PS increase moderately during embryogenesis in control animals.
source: This was accompanied by moderate increases in the levels of major glycerophospholipids like phosphatidylcholine (PC, 13% and 23% at 6–8 hr and 18–20 hr AEL, respectively), phosphatidylethanolamine (PE, 19% and 26% at 6–8 hr and 18–20 hr AEL, respectively), phosphatidylinositol (PI, 21% and 34% at 6–8 hr and 18–20 hr AEL, respectively), and phosphatidylserine (PS, 44% and 54% at 6–8 hr and 18–20 hr AEL, respectively; Figure 6A).
evidence: Shotgun mass spectrometry showed increases in phospholipid levels during embryogenesis as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Sphingolipids and ether-linked glycerophospholipids including Cer, CerPE, and PE O- increase more dramatically during embryogenesis in control animals.
source: Within this time frame, we observed even more pronounced increases in sphingolipids and ether-linked glycerophospholipids including ceramide (Cer, 79% and 75% at 6–8 hr and 18–20 hr AEL, respectively), ceramide phosphoethanolamine (CerPE, 59% and 114% at 6–8 hr and 18–20 hr AEL, respectively), and ether-linked PE (PE O-, 17% and 350% at 6–8 hr and 18–20 hr AEL, respectively; Figure 6A).
evidence: Shotgun mass spectrometry showed substantial increases in sphingolipids and ether lipids during embryogenesis as shown in Figure 6A.

claim: PC, PE, PI, and PS shift toward increased acyl chain length during embryogenesis in control animals.
source: PC, PE, PI, and PS shifted toward increased acyl chain length at 18–20 hr AEL when compared to 0–2 hr AEL (Figure 6B).
evidence: Shotgun mass spectrometry analysis showed changes in lipid molecular composition during embryogenesis as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Hsl1 mutants exhibit similar decreases in TG and increases in membrane lipid levels during embryogenesis as control animals.
source: When compared with control animals, Hsl1 mutants exhibited similar decreases in TG and increases in membrane lipid levels during embryogenesis (Figure 6A,B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Shotgun mass spectrometry showed comparable lipidome remodeling in Hsl1 mutants and controls as shown in Figures 6A, 6B, and supplementary data.

claim: Hsl1 females have 24% and 20% less cumulative egg output than control females after 4 days and 7 days on lipid-depleted medium (LDM), respectively.
source: Hsl1 females had 24% and 20% less cumulative egg output than control females after 4 days and 7 days on LDM, respectively (Figure 7A).
evidence: Fecundity assays showed reduced egg production in Hsl1 mutant females on LDM as shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Hsl1 females produce 37% and 25% less viable progeny than control females within 4 days and 7 days on LDM, respectively.
source: Hsl1 females produced 37% and 25% less viable progeny than control females within 4 days and 7 days on LDM, respectively, indicating slightly higher developmental success of control embryos in the early period on LDM (Figure 7A).
evidence: Fecundity assays showed reduced viable offspring production in Hsl1 mutant females on LDM as shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Dietary cholesterol supplementation partially rescues the fecundity defect of Hsl1 mutant animals.
source: After dietary supplementation with exogenous cholesterol, Hsl1 females showed 16% and 14% lower egg output than control females at 4 days and 7 days, respectively, suggesting that dietary cholesterol partially rescued the fecundity defect of Hsl1 mutant animals (Figure 7B).
evidence: Fecundity assays with cholesterol supplementation showed partial rescue of egg production defects as shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Vitellogenic follicles of Hsl1 females produce numerous lipid droplets at stage 10 of oogenesis.
source: Vitellogenic follicles of control but also Hsl1 females produced numerous LDs at stage 10 of oogenesis suggesting that oocyte lipid loading is generally functional in Hsl1 mutant animals (Figure 7C).
evidence: Microscopy analysis showed normal lipid droplet formation in Hsl1 mutant oocytes as shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Hsl1 mutants transfer 20% and 24% less labeled cholesterol into embryos at 3 days and 4 days after female mating.
source: To more specifically monitor sterol transport, we followed the incorporation of labeled cholesterol into embryos produced by mothers of both genotypes and found that Hsl1 mutants transferred 20% and 24% less labeled cholesterol into the embryos laid at 3 days and 4 days after female mating (Figure 7D).
evidence: Radiolabeling experiments showed reduced maternal sterol transfer to embryos in Hsl1 mutants as shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Fat body-specific knockdown of Hsl expression reduces cumulative egg and 1st instar numbers by 27-29% and 32-34%, respectively, after 4 days on LDM.
source: Fat body-specific knockdown of Hsl expression by means of a Cg-GAL4 driven Hsl shRNA transgene reduced cumulative egg and 1st instar numbers by 27–29% and 32–34%, respectively, after 4 days on LDM as compared to controls harboring either the Hsl shRNA or the Cg-GAL4 only (Figure 7E).
evidence: RNAi-mediated knockdown experiments showed that fat body Hsl is required for optimal fecundity as shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Fat body-specific re-expression of Hsl ameliorates fecundity defects associated with complete Hsl-deficiency.
source: Fat body-specific Hsl re-expression was sufficient to ameliorate fecundity defects associated with complete Hsl-deficiency (14% less eggs and 8% less 1st instar larvae compared to controls at 4 days on LDM, Figure 7F).
evidence: Tissue-specific rescue experiments showed that fat body Hsl expression improves fecundity in Hsl1 mutants as shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Hsl is a lipid droplet-associated enzyme in Drosophila fat body cells.
source: Finally, we assessed the subcellular localization of a fluorescently-tagged version of Hsl (Hsl-EGFP) in fat body cells of adult flies and found that Hsl-EGFP concentrated at the surface of LDs (Figure 1D).
evidence: The localization of Hsl-EGFP to lipid droplet surfaces implies that Hsl functions at lipid droplets to hydrolyze stored lipids.

claim: Hsl is not a major regulator of TG metabolism in adult Drosophila.
source: Taken together, these data argue against a function of Hsl in the regulation of TG and energy metabolism in adult Drosophila in parallel or downstream of other lipolytic systems.
evidence: The absence of TG accumulation, normal energy metabolism, and normal starvation response in Hsl1 mutants collectively suggest that Hsl does not play a major role in TG metabolism.

claim: Hsl specifically regulates sterol homeostasis in adult Drosophila by promoting SE catabolism.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Hsl specifically regulates sterol homeostasis in adult Drosophila by promoting the catabolism of SE.
evidence: The combination of SE accumulation, reduced SE hydrolase activity, and slower SE turnover in Hsl1 mutants supports this conclusion.

claim: Hsl acts as an evolutionarily conserved adipocyte-autonomous regulator of SE catabolism.
source: We conclude that Hsl acts as evolutionarily conserved adipocyte-autonomous regulator of SE catabolism and thereby controls whole-body SE levels in Drosophila.
evidence: The parallel findings of SE accumulation in both Drosophila Hsl1 mutants and mouse AHKO adipocytes support evolutionary conservation of Hsl function in SE catabolism.

claim: Loss of Hsl causes impaired conversion of SE to free sterols during embryogenesis.
source: This suggests that loss of Hsl causes impaired conversion of SE to free sterols during embryogenesis.
evidence: The observation that Hsl1 mutant embryos have both elevated SE and reduced free sterols indicates impaired SE-to-free sterol conversion.

claim: Maternal Hsl autonomously controls embryonic SE catabolism through germline function.
source: Since embryonic SE catabolism was essentially dependent on the maternal genotype, we next asked if germline Hsl autonomously controls embryonic SE catabolism. To this end, we re-expressed Hsl specifically in the germline of mutant animals using the nos-GAL4 driver. Enzyme assays revealed a 72% decrease in embryonic SE hydrolysis rates of Hsl1 as compared to control animals, which was largely reverted by re-expressing Hsl in the germline of mutant mothers (Figure 5C). This indicates that our strategy was successful in restoring active Hsl enzyme in mutant embryos. Germline-specific expression of Hsl fully prevented the SE accumulation in Hsl1 mutant embryos but not in mothers consistent with a germline-autonomous role of the enzyme in SE catabolism (Figure 5C).
evidence: The rescue of embryonic but not maternal SE levels by germline-specific Hsl expression indicates that maternal Hsl acts autonomously in the germline to control embryonic SE catabolism.

claim: Decreased sterols as a consequence of defective SE catabolism are largely compatible with normal remodeling of membrane lipids in Hsl1 mutant embryos.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that (1) Hsl acts as specific regulator of sterols but not of other lipids during embryogenesis and (2) decreased sterols as a consequence of defective SE catabolism are largely compatible with normal remodeling of membrane lipids in Hsl1 mutant embryos.
evidence: The similar lipidome remodeling patterns in control and Hsl1 mutant embryos despite reduced free sterols suggests that embryonic membrane lipid metabolism can proceed normally with reduced sterol levels.

claim: Optimal egg production and reproductive success requires Hsl-mediated SE catabolism in the fat body of mothers, particularly when dietary sterol is limited.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that optimal egg production and reproductive success requires Hsl-mediated SE catabolism in the fat body of the mothers, particularly when dietary sterol is limited.
evidence: The fecundity defects on LDM, partial rescue by cholesterol supplementation, and rescue by fat body-specific Hsl expression collectively support this conclusion.

claim: Hsl promotes efficient sterol transfer from mothers to progeny.
source: This suggests that Hsl indeed promotes the mobilization and transfer of maternal sterols to the progeny.
evidence: The reduced transfer of labeled cholesterol to embryos in Hsl1 mutants indicates that Hsl facilitates maternal-to-embryo sterol transfer.

claim: The Hsl1 deletion mutant lacks 2.74 kb genomic Hsl sequences, including most of the open-reading frame and the start codon.
source: To investigate the role of Hsl in organismal lipid metabolism, we used imprecise P-element excision to generate the Hsl1 deletion mutant, which lacks 2.74 kb genomic Hsl sequences, including most of the open-reading frame and the start codon (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The genomic structure of the Hsl1 allele is described and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Hsl1 deletion results in the absence of detectable Hsl mRNA.
source: This results in the absence of detectable Hsl mRNA whereas mRNA concentrations of the neighboring genes Ate1 and PCNA are unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: qPCR analysis showed loss of Hsl mRNA in Hsl1 mutants as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Metazoan Hsl enzyme family members are characterized by a N-terminal Hsl_N domain and a C-terminal α/β hydrolase fold three domain interspersed with a regulatory module.
source: Metazoan Hsl enzyme family members, including human and fly Hsl, are characterized by a N-terminal Hsl_N domain (PF06350) and a C-terminal part composed of a α/β hydrolase fold three domain (PF07859) interspersed with a regulatory module.
evidence: The structural organization of Hsl family members is described based on domain architecture.

claim: Substrate promiscuity covering a wide range of neutral lipids including TG and SE is a common feature of Hsl-related proteins.
source: Substrate promiscuity covering a wide range of neutral lipids including TG and SE is a common feature of Hsl-related proteins (Lass et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lass et al., 2011.

claim: Mammalian Hsl is a TG and major DG lipase in adipocytes where it acts in parallel and downstream of ATGL.
source: In fact, Hsl is a TG and major DG lipase in mammalian adipocytes where it acts in parallel and downstream of ATGL to promote storage lipid breakdown (Lass et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lass et al., 2011.

claim: Mouse Hsl acts as major SE hydrolase in liver, intestine, testis, and adrenal gland.
source: In addition, mouse Hsl acts as major SE hydrolase in several tissues including liver, intestine, testis, and adrenal gland (Kraemer et al., 2004; Obrowsky et al., 2012; Osuga et al., 2000; Sekiya et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kraemer et al., 2004; Obrowsky et al., 2012; Osuga et al., 2000; Sekiya et al., 2008.

claim: Mammalian Hsl activity is stimulated by catabolic hormones such as glucagon or catecholamines.
source: Mammalian Hsl activity is stimulated by catabolic hormones such as glucagon or catecholamines (Lass et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lass et al., 2011.

claim: Drosophila shares many principles of metabolism and physiology with higher organisms.
source: The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster (hereafter referred to as Drosophila) shares many principles of metabolism and physiology with higher organisms and is gaining increasing popularity as a model organism for research in lipid metabolism and related metabolic diseases (Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Musselman and Kühnlein, 2018.

claim: Drosophila is unable to de novo synthesize sterol lipids.
source: In particular, Drosophila is unable to de novo synthesize sterol lipids, which are important membrane constituents and precursors for protein modification and molting hormones (Carvalho et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Carvalho et al., 2010.

claim: Brummer (Bmm) lipase is the ortholog of mammalian adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL) and a major regulator of basal and starvation-induced TG lipolysis in Drosophila.
source: Brummer (Bmm) lipase is the ortholog of mammalian adipose triglyceride lipase (ATGL) and a major regulator of basal and starvation-induced TG lipolysis (Grönke et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grönke et al., 2005.

claim: The acid lipase family member Magro controls SE hydrolysis in the enterocytes of the Drosophila midgut.
source: The acid lipase family member Magro has been shown to control SE hydrolysis in the enterocytes of the midgut (Sieber and Thummel, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sieber and Thummel, 2012.

claim: Hsl is expressed throughout Drosophila development with particularly high levels during early embryogenesis.
source: Hsl is expressed throughout development with particularly high levels during early embryogenesis (Bi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bi et al., 2012.

claim: SE accumulation is a characteristic of Hsl-deficient cells across phyla including murine white adipocytes.
source: Notably, accumulation of SE but not of TG is a characteristic of Hsl-deficient cells across phyla including murine white adipocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the parallel observations in Drosophila and mouse adipocytes presented in the study.

claim: Hsl improves intergenerational sterol transfer and reproductive success in flies.
source: In summary, we identified Hsl as an ancestral regulator of SE degradation, which improves intergenerational sterol transfer and reproductive success in flies.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study regarding Hsl function in reproduction.
